newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Peace returns to PNG, but fears linger over army role.
newsitem.headline: Peace returns to PNG, but fears linger over army role.

text.p: A large, shining cross stands on a hill overlooking the army's Murray barracks in Port Moresby.

For many Papua New Guineans the cross, erected for the Christian holiday of Easter, has become a symbol of hope after this South Pacific nation weathered its worst political crisis in 22 years of independence.

Peace has returned to Port Moresby after Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan stepped down on Wednesday in the face of an army mutiny and angry street protests over his plan to use mercenaries to quell a rebellion on Bougainville island.
But the incident has raised fears about the future role of the 4,000-strong defence force in politics.
"This is the first time in 22 years of our independence that the military has been involved in any political debate," said Post-Courier newspaper editor Oseah Philemon.
"The precedent has been set. It could happen again.

"We were lucky this time because (sacked defence force commander Brigadier-General) Jerry Singirok ... was able to contain the soldiers and they were loyal to him. It may not be the same in the future.
"This is the worrying thing because some other commander in many years down the track will say well, they got close to doing it, perhaps we'll get a little further this time."

The crisis erupted when Singirok condemned Chan's plan to use mercenaries to quell the rebellion on Bougainville. Singirok demanded Chan step down and an inquiry into the awarding of the $36 million contract.
Chan sacked Singirok, but opposition to the deal sparked street protests and an army mutiny.
Other analysts, while concerned that the precedent of army involvement in politics had been set, were more optimistic.
"I don't think there's any reason to be alarmist," said Jim Griffin emeritus professor of history at the University of PNG.
"The military are not going to intervene on a month-by-month basis simply because they were able to intervene on this occasion," he told Reuters by phone from his home in Canberra.
Most analysts and politicians agree that Papua New Guinea's democratic institutions have survived for the time being and that parliament's supremacy was upheld.
"The events of the last fortnight have clearly indicated that Papua New Guinea is not Africa," Griffin said.
The country's founding prime minister and a leader of the parliamentary push to oust Chan, Sir Michael Somare, said the political system had not been wrecked.
"It proves Papua New Guinea's institutions work, rather than that they have failed," he told Reuters.
Vital to protecting the system was parliament's vote against a motion calling for Chan's ousting, while an angry mob that included armed soldiers rallied outside demanding he quit.
"It was very important that the parliament not be seen giving into this kind (of action)," a long-time PNG watcher told Reuters.
But many fear the root tensions behind this month's mutiny and popular uprising remain.
"There is always the chance of this sort of thing happening as long as corruption remains a way of life in politics," said one Port Moresby-based diplomat.

"And while the politicians get richer and the army continues to be treated appallingly -- problems with pay, food, housing that falls down around them -- a lot of ordinary soldiers are going to stay very, very angry."
Caretaker Prime Minister John Giheno, regarded as a competent but not outstanding leader, has pledged greater transparency in a bid to meet public concerns.

"I think it's a general question (about) ... transparency in the government that forced the army and the public to go the way they did," he told Reuters. "Whatever we do at the political level, we must improve that transparency."
Further clouding the future of this rugged nation of almost 4.5 million people is a national election scheduled for June.
The abolition of provincial government means a record number of candidates are expected to stand for national parliament.

With PNG's first-past-the-post voting system, that means candidates can be elected with only a fraction of the vote, injecting further uncertainty in the already fluid and unpredictable politics of this nation.
Only 55 of the 109 current parliamentarians won more than 20 percent of the vote in their electorate and nine were elected with less than 10 percent.
"It's a chaotic democracy," said the PNG-watcher.
Like Chan's administration, the next government will be a coalition, but no one here is willing to predict its make-up.
Whatever the outcome of the poll, few regard Chan as politically dead, despite the crisis.
"Julius will be back in the parliament. If he's back in the parliament, he's going to be an influential figure in some way," said the PNG watcher.
